sections.h2: What are my options for selling a house in Pemberton, NJ?
sections.html:
A Pemberton owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who takes the house as it stands. The right route depends on how fast you need to close and how much work the township will want done before it signs off on the transfer.

Pemberton Township covers about 62 square miles of Burlington County, which makes it the fourth largest of the county's 40 municipalities by area. Its communities include Browns Mills, Country Lake Estates, Pemberton Heights, Presidential Lakes Estates and a slice of Fort Dix. The borough of Pemberton sits inside the township as one of New Jersey's doughnut towns, so confirm which Pemberton your address belongs to before you download any forms.

  • Listing with an agent: the widest buyer pool, but you carry showings, a buyer's inspection and the township's own resale inspection.
  • Selling on your own: you save the listing commission and take on pricing, marketing and the paperwork the township tax office and code office expect.
  • Cash sale as-is: fewer moving parts and a short closing window, with the price reflecting the repairs the buyer takes on.

sections.h2: What does the Pemberton housing market look like for sellers?
sections.html:
Pemberton is a mostly owner-occupied township with home values well below the national figure. The Census Bureau estimated 27,611 residents on July 1, 2025, up from the 26,903 counted in the 2020 census, and it lists 9,785 households averaging 2.73 people.

For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied homes in Pemberton at $234,500, against $332,700 for the United States. Owners occupy 73.3 percent of homes, median household income is $80,843, and workers spend a mean of 31.7 minutes getting to their jobs. About 16.6 percent of residents are 65 or older.

Getting around Pemberton means county and state roads. County Route 530, Route 70 in the south and U.S. Route 206 along the western edge carry most traffic, while Interstate 295 and the New Jersey Turnpike lie outside the township in neighboring Springfield, two towns away from the nearest interchanges. NJ Transit bus route 317 links the area with Asbury Park and Philadelphia. Pemberton Township's schools run through one district for most of the township, with nine schools and 4,443 students in the 2021 to 2022 school year.

sections.h2: Does a Pemberton house need an inspection before it sells?
sections.html:
Yes. Pemberton requires a Certificate of Occupancy Transfer each time a residential dwelling unit changes occupant, and a sale triggers it. The seller files a resale application with the Code Enforcement office and pays an inspection fee.

The township's resale packet lists a $150 fee for the first inspection and $50 for each reinspection. Nobody schedules an inspection without a completed application and the fee paid in full, and fees are taken at the housing office rather than by inspectors in the field. An application expires after 60 days, so file it close to your target closing rather than months ahead.

If the buyer is taking over the certificate, Pemberton asks that the office be told in writing before the transfer certificate is issued. That matters in an as-is sale, where the buyer often wants to handle repairs after closing. Code Enforcement can be reached at 609-894-3376.

  • Reflective house numbers at least 3.5 inches high, readable from the street.
  • Battery-operated smoke detectors on each level and in and outside sleeping areas, plus carbon monoxide detectors near bedrooms when the home has a fuel-burning device or attached garage.
  • An anti-tilt device on the stove, handrails on stairs of four or more risers, and an ABC fire extinguisher between 5 and 10 pounds.
  • Screens on windows, working egress windows, and GFCI protection on kitchen, bathroom, garage and exterior outlets.
  • Utilities turned on during the inspection.

sections.h2: What else does the Pemberton resale application check?
sections.html:
The application checks the account side of the property as well as the building. Departments initial boxes for open balances, so clearing them early keeps the file moving.

  • The tax office confirms liens, taxes paid, and the solid waste, water and sewer accounts.
  • Public Works records the sewer and water account units billed.
  • The housing office looks for open construction permits, open code violations, vacant property fees and any board-up or clean-up charges.
  • Homes on a well or septic system attach a well report or septic report.

Some limits are spelled out in the township's checklist. It does not inspect air conditioning, pools, hot tubs or termites, does not review wet basements with standing water, and does not haul away unwanted furniture or appliances. Certifications from a bonded contractor may be requested for the roof, electrical, structural or heating systems.

sections.h2: How do Pemberton property taxes work at closing?
sections.html:
Pemberton bills in four quarterly installments due February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a ten-day grace period to the 10th. Miss the grace period and interest runs from the first of the month, at 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent above that, plus a 6 percent year-end penalty on balances still open at December 31.

The bill covers the township, Burlington County, the county farmland and open space fund, the Pemberton Township Board of Education and the county library. The township collects for all of them, which is why a tax search matters at closing. Payments count on the date received, not the postmark, so allow mailing time for any quarter that falls near your closing date. The tax office answers at 609-894-3370 for bills that never arrived, and a missing bill does not excuse a payment.

If a lien is on the property, only a party with a legal interest can redeem it. Requests go in writing to TaxOffice@pemberton-twp.com, redemption must be paid in full with certified funds, and partial payments are refused. A title company normally handles this at closing.

sections.h2: Do Pinelands rules matter when selling in Pemberton?
sections.html:
They can, because Pemberton lies inside the Pinelands National Reserve and part of the township falls in the state-designated Pinelands Area. The reserve was created by Congress in 1978 and covers about 1.1 million acres across southern New Jersey.

For an existing house that is simply changing hands, the effect is usually small. It becomes real when a buyer or seller plans an addition, a new outbuilding or a lot split. Ask the township's Community Development office whether your parcel sits in the Pinelands Area before you promise a buyer anything beyond the existing footprint.

sections.h2: What do New Jersey and Burlington County add to a Pemberton sale?
sections.html:
New Jersey charges the seller a realty transfer fee when the deed is recorded. For a sale of $350,000 or less the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 on the next $50,000 and $3.90 per $500 on the portion between $200,000 and $350,000. Using the Census median value of $234,500, that works out to about $1,204.

A Gross Income Tax form also goes with every deed. Nonresident sellers pay an estimated tax at closing, calculated on the gain at the top rate but never less than 2 percent of the price recited in the deed. Pemberton owners who live elsewhere, including heirs who moved away, should expect this line on the settlement sheet.

Burlington County Clerk's Office records the deed. It requires the most recent version of the state's seller tax declaration for forms signed on or after October 1, 2025, and runs a free property fraud alert that emails or texts an owner whenever a document is recorded in their name. Sign up through the county clerk, or call 609-265-5122. The county names seniors and owners of vacant properties as frequent targets of deed fraud.

sections.h2: When does a cash offer make sense for a Pemberton house?
sections.html:
A cash offer fits when the house needs more than the township checklist allows, when the property is vacant, or when a closing date matters more than the last dollar of price. Because Pemberton ties every change of occupant to a Certificate of Occupancy Transfer, ask any buyer up front who orders the inspection, who pays the $150, and who accepts responsibility for the repair list.

Compare a cash offer against an agent listing by what you net after repairs, carrying costs and the realty transfer fee, not against the headline price. A home with open permits or unpaid sewer and solid waste accounts can still sell, but those items must be settled or credited at closing.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell my house in Pemberton Township?
faqs.a: Yes. Pemberton requires a Certificate of Occupancy Transfer whenever a residential unit changes occupant. The resale application carries a $150 inspection fee, a $50 reinspection fee and a 60 day life.

faqs.q: Can the buyer handle the Pemberton certificate instead of me?
faqs.a: Yes, if the code office is told in writing before the transfer certificate is issued. The buyer then takes on the repair list, which is common in as-is and investor purchases.

faqs.q: When are Pemberton property taxes due?
faqs.a: Quarterly, on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, with a grace period to the 10th. Interest is 8 percent on the first $1,500 of delinquency and 18 percent above it, and the tax office can give a payoff figure for closing.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Pemberton sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. At a sale price equal to the Census median home value of $234,500, the state's rate table gives about $1,204.

faqs.q: Does Pemberton Borough follow the same sale rules as the township?
faqs.a: Ask before assuming. The borough is a separate municipality inside the township, and the resale application and tax dates quoted here come from the township. Call the code office that covers your address to confirm which one applies.
